title: The One With Ross And Monicas Cousin

jokes.text: Joey practices blowing off his friend before even getting the part
jokes.setup: Friend asks 'How was your audition?' as a normal greeting
jokes.punchline: Joey pretends not to know them, explaining he's 'practicing blowing you off' because he's going to be a movie star — before he's even gotten the part
jokes.explanation: Perfect Joey character comedy — his delusional self-confidence and anticipatory celebrity behavior is entirely on-brand. The reveal that he hasn't even gotten the part yet is the ideal kicker. Strong character integration elevates what could be a simple gag.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm practicing being rude to people because when I become famous, I'm gonna have to be a jerk to them.

jokes.text: The 'next-next Martin Scorsese' explanation
jokes.setup: Joey calls the director 'the next-next Martin Scorsese,' a strange phrase that invites a question
jokes.punchline: Chandler asks, Joey explains there's already a 'next Scorsese' in Chicago, so this guy is right after him — a logical but absurd hierarchy
jokes.explanation: A clever observational joke about Hollywood hyperbole. The logic is airtight and the deadpan delivery of a ridiculous ranking system lands well. Not a huge laugh but consistently clever writing.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: This guy is like, the next Spielberg!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: The next Spielberg? What does that mean? There's only one Spielberg.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No, no, he's like, you know, the next great director. Like after Spielberg.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: So... the second Spielberg?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah! Exactly!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Joey, that's just called being a director.

jokes.text: Joey's response to being asked about full-frontal nudity: 'Are you kidding me? I never rent a movie without it!'
jokes.setup: Estelle asks Joey if he has a problem with full-frontal nudity, expecting hesitation
jokes.punchline: Joey enthusiastically confirms he loves full-frontal nudity in movies, completely missing that he's being asked about his OWN nudity
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The double meaning is perfectly set up — the question could mean either thing — and Joey's answer reveals his complete obliviousness while also being deeply in character (he's a perv who loves nude movies AND someone so self-absorbed he doesn't consider it means himself). Tight, quotable, and character-specific. The 'Oh' follow-up beat as it registers is the perfect button.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Okay, so like, 'next' is the person after this one, right? And 'next-next' is the person after that person. It's simple math!

jokes.text: 'My grandmother's gonna see this.' / 'Grandma's gonna have to get in line.'
jokes.setup: Joey expresses concern about his grandmother seeing his nude scene
jokes.punchline: Chandler suggests the grandmother will have competition for seeing Joey naked — implying a large and enthusiastic audience
jokes.explanation: Sharp, economical comeback. Chandler's wit at its best — takes a straight line and flips it into something absurd and funny. The implication is both a compliment to Joey and a jab at his vanity. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.line: Do you have a problem with full-frontal nudity?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No, no, I love it!

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.line: Great, because this role requires it.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh! Oh, wait, wait. No, no, no. I thought you meant in movies. I don't want to do it myself.

jokes.text: Chandler's 'no sex pact' joke: 'I have one of those with every woman in America'
jokes.setup: Monica mentions their 'no sex before the wedding' pact to Chandler
jokes.punchline: Chandler deadpans that he effectively has the same pact with every woman in America — a self-deprecating joke about his prior romantic failures
jokes.explanation: Excellent Chandler self-deprecation. The joke recontextualizes 'no sex pact' from a romantic gesture into a reflection of his historically dismal love life. Tight, well-constructed, deeply character-specific. One of his better lines in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: My grandmother's gonna see me naked!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Hey, look on the bright side - at least a million people will finally get to see what they've been asking for.

jokes.text: Ross wondering if Cassie still carries a Barbie, then almost revealing he still carries one too
jokes.setup: Ross wonders aloud if Cassie, now 25, still carries a Barbie doll everywhere
jokes.punchline: Monica points out Cassie is 25; Ross starts 'So? I still...' before catching himself — implying he still carries a Barbie
jokes.explanation: Classic interrupted-admission joke. The structure is perfectly executed — the half-sentence is funnier than any full reveal could be. Ross's manchild qualities are well-established so the character integration is high. Monica's dry 'You're probably right' button is pitch-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I can't believe we're doing this. A no-sex pact? Monica, I'm thrilled! Finally, someone's making it easy for me.

jokes.text: Monica calling out the guys' 'subtle' attempt to separate her for the surprise shower planning
jokes.setup: Phoebe asks to speak to Rachel privately — an obvious ploy to plan the shower
jokes.punchline: Monica immediately says 'Subtle, guys' — she already knows they're planning her surprise bridal shower
jokes.explanation: Functional situational comedy. Monica's hyper-awareness is in character, and the ironic delivery is clean. Not a standout but it moves the scene with a smile.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Do they still make Barbie dolls?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I... I wouldn't know.

jokes.text: Rachel and Phoebe's horrified realization: 'We have to throw her a shower?'
jokes.setup: Monica asks them to just play along with the surprise shower they were supposedly planning
jokes.punchline: The moment she leaves, Rachel or Phoebe whispers 'We have to throw her a shower?' — revealing they had no actual plan
jokes.explanation: Good reveal comedy — the gap between what Monica thinks is happening and the reality is immediately exposed. The timing (the second she leaves) is key. Broad but effective.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, you guys are planning a surprise shower for me?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, we were... but actually, we haven't planned anything yet.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What do you mean you haven't planned anything?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I mean, we were just talking about planning it. We got as far as deciding to plan it, but then we didn't actually plan it.

jokes.text: 'That's what you say about porn' — Chandler's response to Joey claiming nudity is 'important to the story'
jokes.setup: Joey insists this is a serious film and nudity is 'really important to the story'
jokes.punchline: Chandler flatly notes that's exactly what people say to justify porn
jokes.explanation: Sharp, economical Chandler retort. It punctures Joey's self-delusion with perfect efficiency. The joke has a timeless quality — this exact exchange happens in real life constantly. Very well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's the universal porn excuse!

jokes.text: Joey finishes describing the tender barn love scene and Chandler adds: 'Plus, everyone will see your thing!'
jokes.setup: Joey waxes poetic about his character — Catholic boy, Jewish girl, rainstorm, barn, 'really sweet and tender'
jokes.punchline: Chandler cuts through all the romanticism with the blunt reality: 'Plus, everyone will see your thing!'
jokes.explanation: Excellent structure. Joey's earnest, increasingly romantic description creates a long setup that Chandler demolishes with one crude but perfectly timed line. The contrast between the buildup and the blunt punchline is what makes it land so hard. Good laugh-out-loud moment.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: And then I slowly remove her dress, and I kiss her neck, and we fall onto the bed together...

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: And then you wake up.

jokes.text: The shower planning rapid-fire sequence, culminating in Phoebe suggesting 'Lusts of the Flesh!' as a party theme
jokes.setup: Rachel and Phoebe are speed-planning the shower — location, time, food — in rapid-fire agreement
jokes.punchline: When asked for a theme, Phoebe blurts 'Lusts of the Flesh!' — a wildly inappropriate suggestion for a bridal shower
jokes.explanation: Perfect Phoebe moment. The rapid-fire sequence creates momentum and an expectation of sensible answers, which Phoebe then completely destroys. The specific absurdity of 'Lusts of the Flesh' as a phrase — almost biblical, definitely unhinged — is what makes it special rather than any generic weird answer.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, you know, I was born yesterday. Well, not yesterday yesterday, but my birth certificate says I was born in 1967, so technically I'm older than I think I am, which is actually pretty cool when you think about it. But anyway, the point is, yesterday is totally possible. I've been there. Multiple times.

jokes.text: The chili negotiation: 'Finger sandwiches and tea. Great! Very Monica.' / 'And chili!' / 'You went one too far.'
jokes.setup: They agree on finger sandwiches and tea for the shower — perfectly Monica-appropriate
jokes.punchline: Phoebe adds 'And chili!' Rachel shoots it down: 'You went one too far.' — implying this is a bridge too far even for Phoebe's eccentricities
jokes.explanation: Nicely economical joke. 'You went one too far' is a reusable phrase that captures the comedic principle of one escalation past the acceptable limit. Good character work from Rachel as the straight man here.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I can't do this! The flowers are wrong, the caterer cancelled, and Monica's going to kill me!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Rachel, you need to calm down.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I AM calm!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: No, you need to be calm. Like, actually calm.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Phoebe, I am literally the calmest I have ever been!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: That's the problem.

jokes.text: The flowers/balloons/neither negotiation
jokes.setup: Phoebe suggests both flowers AND balloons; Rachel reminds her they're paying for it
jokes.punchline: Phoebe immediately pivots to 'Neither' — the full 180 from excess to nothing
jokes.explanation: Quick functional gag built on the comedic rule of threes and the 180-degree pivot. Lightweight but gets a chuckle. Part of the broader rapid-fire sequence that works better as a whole.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: We could do chili!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Phoebe, no. This is an elegant shower. We're doing bruschetta and crostini.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: But people love chili.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Not at a bridal shower, they don't.

jokes.text: Chandler proposes they fake a breakup so they can have sex before the wedding
jokes.setup: Both pretend they're glad about the no-sex pact; Chandler's desire is building
jokes.punchline: He suggests manufacturing a fake fight and 'breaking up for a few hours' to get a loophole around the pact
jokes.explanation: The situational comedy of trying to find a loophole in a self-imposed rule is a relatable and well-trodden sitcom premise, but the specific execution here — immediately caving to propose the breakup — is characteristically Chandler. Solid if not spectacular.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh! Oh! How about a "baby's first lethal injection" theme?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Or we could do something with a tire iron and a bucket of eels!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, I got it. A nice Scandinavian furniture theme!

jokes.text: Monica and Chandler's mock-insult names during the fake breakup: 'bossy and domineering' / 'sloppy and immature'
jokes.setup: They agree to fake a fight to have a loophole for sex; Chandler addresses Monica
jokes.punchline: He calls her 'bossy and domineering,' she calls him 'sloppy and immature' — accurate insults that also function as terms of endearment in this context
jokes.explanation: Good character work — these are literally the most accurate descriptors of these two characters, used as insults in a romantic context. The layers (accurate + insulting + affectionate) give it some depth.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You're shrill!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Shrill? SHRILL?! Out of all the things you could have said, you picked the one word that actually hurts!

jokes.text: The wedding is back on because Chandler called Monica 'shrill'
jokes.setup: Monica and Chandler are enjoying their fake breakup game; Chandler escalates by calling her 'obsessive and shrill'
jokes.punchline: Monica snaps 'Shrill? The wedding is back on' — she's genuinely offended by 'shrill' specifically, ending the game
jokes.explanation: Smart escalation with an unexpected specific trigger. 'Bossy' and 'domineering' she can take as game, but 'shrill' is a bridge too far — the specificity of that one word being what breaks the bit is very funny and character-specific. Monica's vanity/sensitivity is the core of the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What? I wasn't staring. I was just... appreciating the architectural details of her face. Very symmetrical. It's a geometric thing. I'm very into shapes.

jokes.text: Chandler staring at Cassie — the extended reaction beat and silence after meeting her
jokes.setup: Chandler meets Cassie, Monica's beautiful cousin, and says a polite hello
jokes.punchline: An extended pause (from 06:12 to 06:17) where Chandler visibly cannot stop staring — Monica has to call his name to get him to leave
jokes.explanation: A visual gag that sets up the subsequent jokes about Chandler's staring. The beat itself is fairly stock — man can't stop staring at beautiful woman — but it's well-executed and necessary scaffolding. Gets a rewatch bonus because on rewatch the stare is funnier knowing what follows.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yeah, you were looking at her breasts, Chandler.

jokes.text: 'Pervie Perverson' — Monica's nickname for Chandler after he stares at Cassie
jokes.setup: Monica needs to explain to Rachel why Cassie can't stay with them
jokes.punchline: She refers to Chandler as 'Pervie Perverson' for staring at her cousin
jokes.explanation: The made-up name 'Pervie Perverson' is a genuinely good bit of wordplay — it sounds like a character name from a parody, and Monica's indignation makes it land harder. High quotability because of the specific sound of the name.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I wasn't staring at your aunt. I was just... looking in that direction.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Chandler, she's married. And she's my aunt. You're in dangerous territory here.

jokes.text: Chandler's defense: 'I wasn't staring, I was listening intently. It's called being a good conversationalist.'
jokes.setup: Monica accuses Chandler of staring at Cassie; he's clearly guilty
jokes.punchline: He insists he was 'listening intently' and calls it 'being a good conversationalist' — an absurd euphemism for ogling
jokes.explanation: Classic Chandler defensive double-speak. The reframing of a guilty act as a virtue ('good conversationalist') is a well-executed ironic deflection. His offer to demonstrate it immediately is a good button.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What?! I didn't get the part?!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You know what, I don't even want to hear it. I'm out of here!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: *storms toward the door*

jokes.text: Monica's response to Chandler's 'good conversationalist' claim: 'You were staring about eight inches south of there'
jokes.setup: Chandler asks Monica to 'say something' to demonstrate his listening; she looks at him knowingly
jokes.punchline: She calls out exactly WHERE he was looking — 'eight inches south' of her face
jokes.explanation: Excellent precision comedy. 'Eight inches south' is specific, anatomically suggestive without being crude, and the specificity of the measurement is what sells it. Monica's withering delivery makes it a great comeback. Strong laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait... I knew that the whole time. Yeah, I was just... I was doing a bit. A character choice.

jokes.text: Ross asks what Cassie looks like; Monica says 'exactly like Aunt Marilyn'; Ross immediately asks if Aunt Marilyn is coming to the wedding — 'Wafer-thin ice'
jokes.setup: Monica describes Cassie as looking exactly like their very attractive Aunt Marilyn
jokes.punchline: Ross's immediate reaction is to ask if Aunt Marilyn is coming to the wedding — implying he finds his own aunt attractive. Monica: 'Wafer-thin ice.'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest jokes. The 'Wafer-thin ice' response is an excellent, economical escalation of the standard 'thin ice' phrase that perfectly captures Monica's disgusted-but-contained reaction. Ross's instant interest in the aunt is dark and character-specific (setting up his entire B-plot). The joke is densely structured: one line of setup, one line of punchline, one line of perfect button.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. So you're telling me they cut off the skin? Why would they do that?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: It's a religious thing, man.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh, okay. So it's like... a hat for your... (gestures) ...your thing?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No, Joey, it's not a hat.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Could be! You don't know!

jokes.text: Joey storms in to tell the director off for not calling — 'You made a bad decision and ruined your movie. Good day!' — only to be told the director loved his tape
jokes.setup: Joey thinks he's been passed over and marches in dramatically to confront the casting people
jokes.punchline: His entire indignant speech is immediately deflated by the news that the director loved him
jokes.explanation: Classic Joey bluster-then-reversal. 'Good day!' is a deliberately old-fashioned, theatrical exit line that suits Joey's flair for the dramatic. The structure of buildup-to-instant-deflation is clean. His pivot to 'Wow! Sure! That's great!' is perfect character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: It's like learning a skill. You know, you can't just undo it.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, it's like if I decided to become ambidextrous. I can't just go back to being right-handed.

jokes.text: Joey's meta-theatrical 'And, scene.' after his accidental improv with the casting director
jokes.setup: Joey dramatically stormed in to quit, then discovered he'd actually gotten through — a perfect accidental performance
jokes.punchline: He announces 'And, scene.' as if it was all intentional, then congratulates himself: 'Wasn't that fun? We did a little improv there. Yeah!'
jokes.explanation: One of the best Joey lines in the episode. The self-aware actor-speak ('And, scene') applied to a real-life situation he accidentally stumbled through is perfectly in character — Joey genuinely cannot distinguish between performance and reality, and his shameless ownership of the moment is hilarious. 'We did a little improv there' as if the casting director was his scene partner is gold.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I could help you out. I mean, I'm not a doctor, but I did stay at a Holiday Inn Express last night.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No. But I'm thinking what you need is a full-body exfoliation. You know, get some of that dead skin off. I could use my shower loofah on you.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Dude, that's disgusting!

jokes.text: Joey's concern: 'As long as it's handled tastefully. And that barn is not too cold.'
jokes.setup: Joey agrees to do the nude scene, saying it should be handled 'tastefully'
jokes.punchline: His specific practical concern is that the barn not be too cold — a reference to what happens to male anatomy in the cold
jokes.explanation: Nicely layered joke — 'tastefully' is the responsible actor thing to say, but the barn cold comment is specific, self-serving, and reveals Joey's real concern. The implication is left unspoken which is the right choice. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. You want to use olive loaf? Do you know what's in olive loaf?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: It's a loaf of meat with olives in it. OLIVES, Joey!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I can't even look at you right now.

jokes.text: Joey's confusion about circumcision: 'Bar mitzvah-ed?'
jokes.setup: The casting director is trying to explain diplomatically that the role requires the actor to be uncircumcised. Joey fails to follow the euphemisms.
jokes.punchline: Joey guesses 'Bar mitzvah-ed?' as a synonym for circumcised — revealing his confusion between religious ceremony and medical procedure.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Joey's malapropism isn't random stupidity — it reveals a specific, coherent misunderstanding: he knows circumcision is associated with Jewish religious practice, he just doesn't know the word, so he reaches for the Jewish ceremony he does know. This makes the joke smarter than it first appears. It's perfectly in character, beautifully economical (one word as punchline), and highly quotable. 'Bar mitzvah-ed' as a verb is inherently funny.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, I would, but I'm not sure I have all the right ingredients. I mean, I've got the bread, but I don't know if I can make the meat stay up.

jokes.text: 'Think 13 years earlier, lose the rabbi, add a scalpel'
jokes.setup: Joey guesses 'bar mitzvah-ed' as the euphemism for circumcision
jokes.punchline: Chandler's correction: 'Think 13 years earlier, lose the rabbi, add a scalpel' — a brilliantly economical description of circumcision
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode and one of the finest lines in Friends' run. It's a perfect construction: three parallel adjustments to a culturally specific event that illuminate the comedic comparison without ever using the actual word. '13 years earlier' — logical. 'Lose the rabbi' — lateral but perfect. 'Add a scalpel' — the kicker that makes it land with shock and laughter simultaneously. Near-maximum economy; every word is load-bearing. Completely original formulation. Easily the episode's most quotable line.

jokes.text: 'This is not like learning to ride a horse. This is like learning to grow a turtleneck.'
jokes.setup: Joey argues that actors say yes to anything and figure it out later — like learning to ride a horse
jokes.punchline: Chandler points out that growing foreskin is not the same as a learnable skill: 'like learning to grow a turtleneck'
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke. 'Grow a turtleneck' is an inspired euphemism for foreskin — it has perfect visual logic, is entirely original in its phrasing, and uses the extended metaphor (learning to do something) to create the comparison. The word 'turtleneck' is funny on its own here because of its awkward specificity. Second only to #27 in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Why are you looking at me like that?

dialogue.speaker: Cassie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, stop doing your Chandler impression!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm not doing a Chandler impression, this is just how I'm standing.

jokes.text: Chandler's prosthetics proposal: 'double-sided tape and some sort of luncheon meat'
jokes.setup: Joey desperately needs a solution — he lied about not being circumcised and must pass a physical inspection
jokes.punchline: Chandler, thinking out loud, proposes fashioning a prosthetic from 'double-sided tape and some sort of luncheon meat'
jokes.explanation: Genuinely surprising and absurd. 'Luncheon meat' as the construction material of choice is both disgusting and hilarious — the specificity of 'luncheon meat' over just 'meat' or 'deli meat' adds an extra layer of comedy. The improvised, practical-problem-solving framing ('off the top of my head') makes it even funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Cassie
dialogue.line: You do great impressions. Do me.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: That came out wrong.

jokes.text: Phoebe's shower favor idea: hand-carved mahogany boxes with individual birthstones
jokes.setup: Rachel and Phoebe need to plan party favors quickly for a shower happening tomorrow
jokes.punchline: Phoebe suggests hand-carved mahogany boxes engraved with names and filled with birthstones — an outrageously lavish and time-consuming gift for a 24-hour turnaround
jokes.explanation: Very good Phoebe character comedy. Her complete blindness to practical constraints — suggesting artisanal hand-carved boxes for a next-day party — is perfectly in character. Rachel's deadpan 'Okay. You take care of that' is the ideal button, essentially assigning the impossible task to Phoebe.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: So, uh, how have you been? What's new with you?

dialogue.speaker: Cousin
dialogue.line: Oh, you know, same old same old. Just been really busy with work.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yeah, yeah, that's... that's great. Very... very interesting.

dialogue.speaker: Cousin
dialogue.line: Are you okay? You seem distracted.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What? No, no, I'm completely focused. Totally engaged in this conversation.

dialogue.speaker: Cousin
dialogue.line: You keep staring at my mouth.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I do? No, I wasn't... I was just... you have some, uh, you have a little... it's nothing.

jokes.text: Rachel's response to the mahogany box idea: 'Okay. You take care of that.' — then pivots immediately to the actual problem
jokes.setup: Phoebe has just proposed an impossibly elaborate party favor
jokes.punchline: Rachel simply assigns it to Phoebe and moves on, treating the insane suggestion as resolved — the comedy is in the complete bypassing of logic
jokes.explanation: Good reaction beat that works as a button for the mahogany box joke. The comedy is in Rachel's weary pragmatism — she's decided to pick her battles. Functional and well-timed.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I know I'm slow to realize things.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: But I can picture our kids now, sitting in class, their teacher asking 'Who can tell me what year Columbus discovered America?' and they're just staring blankly, and I'm thinking, 'That's my boy.'

jokes.text: Ross checking out the deli meats: Turkey? Cheese? Olive loaf? 'Are you making him a sandwich?' / 'No, it's more like a wrap.'
jokes.setup: Chandler is raiding the fridge for materials to construct Joey's prosthetic; Ross watches him reject various meats
jokes.punchline: Ross asks if he's making a sandwich; Chandler says 'No, it's more like a wrap' — technically true but completely misleading
jokes.explanation: Excellent use of misdirection. 'It's more like a wrap' is technically accurate about the prosthetic's application while being completely misleading to Ross. The audience knows the double meaning, Ross doesn't — a perfect dramatic irony setup. 'Olive loaf? I hope that won't work' is also a good beat within the sequence.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: People who could attend a party on 24 hours notice? Um, unemployed people and people who are cheating on their significant others.

jokes.text: 'Olive loaf? I hope that won't work.'
jokes.setup: Chandler is going through fridge items as potential prosthetic materials
jokes.punchline: He picks up olive loaf and says 'I hope that won't work' — expressing genuine hope that this particular deli meat won't be the solution, for undignified reasons
jokes.explanation: Very funny specific detail. The implication is that having your friend wear olive loaf in that capacity would be somehow worse than other deli meats — and Chandler's horror at even the possibility is both absurd and completely reasonable. The specificity of 'olive loaf' as the most undignified option does heavy lifting here.

dialogue.speaker: Guest
dialogue.line: I was your accountant four years ago.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, yes! I remember you!

dialogue.speaker: Guest
dialogue.line: Well, I've been meaning to call you. I'm worried about your current tax situation.

jokes.text: Rachel pulls Monica's address book from her purse: 'You're amazing. Did you pull that out of her purse?' / 'Uh-huh. And a little seed money for the party.'
jokes.setup: They need a guest list desperately; Rachel produces Monica's address book
jokes.punchline: Rachel confirms she pickpocketed Monica, and also stole cash for the party — presented with complete cheerfulness
jokes.explanation: Good escalation joke — stealing the address book is already a bit much, but stealing cash too (called 'seed money' as if it's legitimate fundraising) escalates it perfectly. The casualness of 'uh-huh' as the confirmation makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So for your fake anatomy, we could use toothpicks and glue.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Toothpicks and glue? What am I, a kindergarten art project?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, it's either that or we tell people you're a puppet.

jokes.text: Cassie mentions the last time she saw Ross he was setting up a tent in line for Return of the Jedi — and he clearly pretended not to see her that day
jokes.setup: Cassie recalls the last time she saw Ross — he was camping out for Return of the Jedi
jokes.punchline: She notes 'you did see me that day — because it seemed like you didn't' — exposing that Ross hid from her to avoid being seen as a Star Wars nerd
jokes.explanation: Good character-specific embarrassment comedy. The image of Ross camping in line for Jedi is perfectly on-brand, and the fact that he saw her and pretended not to — preferring to be invisible rather than be caught — is a nice character revelation. Cassie recounting this warmly while Ross squirms is well-played.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, I may have made one for myself.

jokes.text: Cassie tells Ross that Chandler 'sure stares a lot' — a callback to his earlier behavior
jokes.setup: Cassie stayed at Monica's; Chandler was established as unable to stop staring at her
jokes.punchline: Cassie innocently mentions this to Ross, confirming Chandler's behavior was visible and notable
jokes.explanation: Functional callback that confirms the earlier visual joke. Cassie's obliviousness to why he was staring, combined with her casual reporting of it, is a nice light touch. Sets up the irony of Ross's own reaction to follow.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Ow! Ow! Ow!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What is that?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: It's a prosthetic nose made of toothpicks.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Why would they make it out of toothpicks?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I don't know, but it hurts!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, try this one.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What is it?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: It's a Fruit Roll-up.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: A Fruit Roll-up? Why would they... Oh my God, this is delicious!

jokes.text: Ross's extended silent staring at Cassie — a visual reaction beat mirroring Chandler's earlier behavior
jokes.setup: Ross was just told Chandler couldn't stop staring at Cassie
jokes.punchline: Ross himself falls into an extended stare — doing the exact thing he's just been told Chandler did; the irony is entirely visual
jokes.explanation: Well-constructed parallel — the audience immediately recognizes that Ross is doing exactly what Chandler was just criticized for. The irony is clean and the structure (warning about behavior immediately followed by the warned behavior) is a solid comedic principle executed well here. Gets rewatch bonus because on rewatch the echo is very satisfying.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, she's just a student. She's off-limits. I'm a professor, I have boundaries. I can do this. Just think of her as... a file. A very attractive file with great legs and...

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No! No, stop it! This isn't working.

jokes.text: Ross does a spot-on impression of Chandler's staring to Cassie's delight
jokes.setup: Cassie laughs at something; Ross is performing an impression to entertain her
jokes.punchline: He does a Chandler impression involving the stare — Cassie loves it, while the audience knows Ross is doing the same thing he's imitating
jokes.explanation: The meta-layer of Ross doing an impression of staring while himself about to stare is a nice bit of layered irony. The character's unawareness of his own hypocrisy is well-played.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: She's flirting with me! Did you see how she touched my arm? That's a classic flirting move.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Ross, she touches everyone's arm.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Not like that she doesn't. And did you hear what she said? She said I have 'interesting' taste in movies.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What's wrong with your taste in movies?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Nothing! She was complimenting me. I just showed her my favorite movie - 'Anaconda.'

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Anaconda? That's the sexiest movie ever made.

jokes.text: Chandler's foreskin prototype update: 'How you doing on that... hot dog?'
jokes.setup: Joey is trying on various meat-based prosthetics; Chandler checks in on a specific prototype
jokes.punchline: The pause before 'hot dog' — Chandler clearly cannot believe this is a real sentence he is saying to another adult
jokes.explanation: Brilliant economy. The comedic pause before 'hot dog' — indicated by the ellipsis in the transcript — does enormous work. The whole situation has escalated to the point where Chandler has to ask his best friend how a hot dog is working as a penile prosthetic. His pause is a character saying 'I cannot believe this is my life.' Very funny.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, I've thought about this very carefully, weighed all the pros and cons, and I've decided... no, wait, I've already decided. I'm committed now. It's like the military—once you're in, you're in. There's no backing out. Even if it's a terrible idea, even if I realize five minutes later it was stupid, I have to see it through because I've already told people about it.

jokes.text: Joey: 'I'm all done.' Chandler: 'Thank God.'
jokes.setup: Chandler asks how the hot dog prototype is going
jokes.punchline: Joey is 'all done' with it — meaning he's eaten it. Chandler's relieved 'Thank God' confirms its failure (and the horror of the whole endeavor)
jokes.explanation: Perfectly economical punchline sequence. 'I'm all done' could mean the trial is over OR Joey ate the hot dog (which is clearly what happened, given his food-focused nature). Chandler's 'Thank God' works on multiple levels — relief that it failed, relief at this whole situation, and the implicit confirmation that Joey did indeed eat a prosthetic prototype. Maximum laughs per word.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I was trying to think of something romantic to say, but then I realized I'd been standing here in complete silence for like three minutes, and now it's too late to say anything because whatever I say will sound like I'm breaking an awkward silence, which I am.

jokes.text: Cassie reminds Ross of the summer she pinned him down and tickled him until he cried, then adds 'We're probably too old to do that now.'
jokes.setup: Cassie is innocently reminiscing about their childhood, recalling physical play.
jokes.punchline: 'We're probably too old to do that now' — Cassie's innocent remark about being too old for childhood roughhousing lands as a cringe bombshell given Ross's internal monologue.
jokes.explanation: The joke is entirely about dramatic irony — Cassie means 'that's a kids' game we've grown past' while Ross hears something completely different. The innocent delivery versus the uncomfortable subtext creates genuine cringe comedy. The audience's awareness of the gap between what's meant and what's heard is what makes this land.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: So... did you see the thing about the new dinosaur discovery? They found fossilized remains that suggest they may have had better social skills than me.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Which is... which is really saying something.

jokes.text: Ross's internal monologue: 'I'll always remember that summer... because that's when I realized that we are related. We share genetic material.'
jokes.setup: Cassie says she'll always remember the summer for her freckles. Ross says he'll always remember it too.
jokes.punchline: Ross's reason — the summer he realized they were related — implies this was a turning point where he had to consciously remind himself they were family. The addition of 'We share genetic material' makes it worse by being scientific and therefore clinical.
jokes.explanation: Ross the scientist using 'we share genetic material' as a mantra to suppress attraction is perfect character-specific comedy. The fact that he had to 'realize' they were related that summer implies he was already attracted to her before the realization. Good layered character work.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Monica, I am so sorry about the shower. I didn't mean to flood the bathroom.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Rachel, it's fine. Although, I'm not sure how you managed to break the curtain rod AND clog the drain at the same time.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I know, I know. And then I tried to fix it myself, which apparently made it worse.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You used a plunger on the rod, didn't you?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: How did you—

jokes.text: Ross tells Cassie he only realized they were related 'that summer' — implying he was having non-familial thoughts before the revelation. 'It took you that long to figure it out?' / 'I'm a little slow.' / 'Just as our children would be.'
jokes.setup: Ross explains that the summer they spent together as kids was when he 'realized we are related' — implying he needed that realization
jokes.punchline: He adds 'Just as our children would be' — a horrifying non-sequitur that reveals he is STILL going down an inappropriate mental path about his cousin
jokes.explanation: Genuinely dark and surprising. 'Just as our children would be' is a staggering non-sequitur that reveals Ross is simultaneously trying to reinforce the familial boundary (by saying he's slow) while completely undermining it (by mentally going to children with his cousin). The audience's shocked laugh is well-earned. This is dark subversive comedy at its most precise.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, look on the bright side—at least now I don't have to pretend to like your girlfriend!

jokes.text: Ross adds: 'Just as our children would be.' — immediately catching himself.
jokes.setup: Ross has just said 'we share genetic material' as a way of reminding himself they're cousins.
jokes.punchline: He extends the thought logically — 'Just as our children would be' — a horrifying implication that he's considered the genetic consequences of a hypothetical future with her.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's darkest and most precise jokes. Ross is trying to use science as an antidote to attraction, but the logic breaks down catastrophically when he extends it to 'our children.' The implication is that he's thought past the relationship to its progeny — which means his mental defenses have completely failed. The self-awareness of catching himself makes it worse. Perfectly economical: five words, maximum horror-comedy. Comparably strong to the 8.0 anchor jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: So what are we doing here?

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.line: Just a routine physical examination, Mr. Tribbiani.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh great, I've been working out. You're gonna love this.

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.line: Just relax and we'll start with some basic tests.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, yeah, I'm ready. I've been doing my sit-ups. How many do you want me to do?

jokes.text: Rachel's assessment of the guests who showed up on 24 hours' notice: 'There's a word for people like that: Losers'
jokes.setup: Phoebe and Rachel are bewildered by the assortment of people who actually showed up for a last-minute shower
jokes.punchline: Rachel diagnoses them: anyone available on 24 hours' notice must be a loser — while she herself organized the whole thing on 24 hours' notice
jokes.explanation: Good self-unaware joke in Rachel's snobby register. The irony that she planned this in 24 hours and is judging people for responding in 24 hours is not stated but completely apparent. Rachel's social hierarchy concerns are on-brand. The delivery — 'There's a word for people like that' building to 'Losers' — has good structure.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What? No, no, no. This isn't what it looks like. I was just... I was just checking to make sure it was on straight.

jokes.text: The accountant reveal: 'How do you know Monica?' / 'I was her accountant four years ago.' / 'I'm interested to find out who's been doing her taxes the last four years.'
jokes.setup: Rachel asks a stranger how they know Monica; she was Monica's accountant four years ago
jokes.punchline: Phoebe or Rachel dryly notes they're 'interested to find out' who took over since — the implication being that neither of them knew and Monica's current financial situation is a mystery
jokes.explanation: Light observational joke about the random assortment of guests. The dry delivery of genuine curiosity about Monica's accounting history is a minor but functional gag.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Wait, Cassie? Cassie... Oh my God!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You're... you're that girl from high school!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I can't believe it's you! You look amazing!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: So, um, are you... are you seeing anyone?

jokes.text: Rachel and Phoebe's miscommunication about inviting Monica: 'You didn't tell her?' / 'You were supposed to!' / 'Please tell her to bring a cake!'
jokes.setup: Monica's shower is happening but nobody thought to invite the guest of honor
jokes.punchline: They realize neither told Monica; they argue over whose fault it is, then Phoebe adds 'And please tell her to bring a cake!' — the ultimate practical concern in an impractical situation
jokes.explanation: Good escalation. The absurdity of asking the guest of honor to bring her own cake captures the spirit of the whole subplot's comedic premise (epic incompetence in party planning). 'Please tell her to bring a cake' is Phoebe at her most casually unaware.

jokes.text: Phoebe and Rachel's shower planning disaster: they forgot to invite Monica to her own surprise shower.
jokes.setup: They planned a surprise shower, but neither told Monica to show up.
jokes.punchline: The fundamental failure of the surprise party — that you have to get the guest of honor there — reveals they were so focused on planning they forgot the most basic step.
jokes.explanation: The structural irony is solid — they've made every other preparation but missed the most obvious thing. The 'Tell her to bring a cake!' button adds to the escalating incompetence. Reliable comedy of errors.

jokes.text: The full prosthetics lineup: mushroom cap, bologna, toothpicks, perishable options, pink suede, fur ('that's just for me')
jokes.setup: Chandler has prepared multiple prototype prosthetics for Joey to try
jokes.punchline: The list escalates from somewhat practical (bologna) to absurd (pink suede that shrinks when wet) to Chandler's personal project (fur, 'that's really just for me')
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalation sequence. Each item is funnier than the last. 'Pink suede' is funny. 'It'll shrink when wet' adds a practical concern nobody wanted to think about. 'I did a little something in fur, but that's really just for me' is the perfect personal-project kicker — the implication that Chandler has created a fur version for his own unspecified purposes is bizarre and hilarious. Strong ensemble laugh.

jokes.text: Joey: 'Thanks, you are such a good friend. And this is so weird.'
jokes.setup: Chandler has just presented an array of penile prosthetics for Joey to test
jokes.punchline: Joey's combination of sincere gratitude and mild understatement ('and this is so weird') about an objectively deeply weird situation
jokes.explanation: Good understated button. 'This is so weird' is an enormous understatement for what's happening, which is what makes it funny. Joey's sincere friendship acknowledgment alongside mild acknowledgment of the absurdity is very Joey.

jokes.text: 'Okay, the taffy's too sticky. I was afraid of that.' / 'Toothpick?' / 'Yeah.'
jokes.setup: Joey is testing the taffy prosthetic
jokes.punchline: Chandler anticipated the taffy's adhesive limitations. Joey requires a toothpick for extraction — the horror implied in that need is the joke
jokes.explanation: Very good quick-fire joke. 'I was afraid of that' as a pre-existing concern about taffy's stickiness in this application is funny. The toothpick request with simple 'Yeah' confirmation leaves the horror to the audience's imagination. Great economy.

jokes.text: The Fruit Roll-Up taste test: 'What are you trying now?' / 'The Fruit Roll-Up.' / 'And?' / 'Delicious.'
jokes.setup: Joey is testing various food-based prosthetic materials; Chandler checks in on the Fruit Roll-Up
jokes.punchline: Joey's review of the Fruit Roll-Up as a prosthetic material is simply 'Delicious' — he ate that one too
jokes.explanation: Possibly the funniest beat in the prosthetic sequence. The rhythm of question-and-answer ('And?' / 'Delicious') is perfect — the word 'Delicious' as a one-word answer to a question about prosthetic performance is a classic subverted-expectation joke. Chandler's setup of 'And?' implies he expects a performance review; Joey's 'Delicious' reveals he ate it again. Perfectly in character — Joey's hunger has no context in which it shuts off.

jokes.text: 'We have a winner! The Silly Putty. Not so silly anymore!'
jokes.setup: After multiple failed food prosthetics, they finally find something that works
jokes.punchline: The winner is Silly Putty — Chandler celebrates with 'Not so silly anymore!' — a recontextualization of the product's name
jokes.explanation: The 'Not so silly anymore' line is a genuinely clever wordplay payoff. The escalation of the whole sequence makes this landing feel earned. It's not just a pun — it's a satisfying resolution to an extended comedic problem.

jokes.text: Ross's internal monologue: 'She was the one who suggested opening a bottle of wine... she was the one who turned down the lights... she was the one that wanted to rent Logan's Run — the sexiest movie ever.'
jokes.setup: Ross is trying to talk himself out of his attraction to his cousin Cassie
jokes.punchline: His internal rationalization that she's sending signals includes calling Logan's Run 'the sexiest movie ever' — a 1970s sci-fi film nobody would describe that way
jokes.explanation: Excellent character comedy. The internal monologue format is used to expose Ross's self-delusion at its most extreme. 'Logan's Run — the sexiest movie ever' is perfect — it's deeply Ross (a nerdy sci-fi movie), and his self-serving reinterpretation of mundane events as signals is precisely the kind of motivated reasoning the character specializes in. High character specificity and quotability.

jokes.text: Ross mentally resolves 'I'm going in' — the extended silent decision to make a move on his cousin
jokes.setup: Ross has convinced himself through increasingly tortured logic that his cousin wants him
jokes.punchline: He mentally resolves to act on it — the horror/comedy of his actual intention becoming clear as he stands up to approach her
jokes.explanation: Good sustained cringe build. The audience's horror at Ross's decision makes this land as a cringe-comedy beat. The gap between how he sees the situation and reality is at maximum here.

jokes.text: Ross's internal voice: 'Oh my God, this is the longest that anyone has not talked ever!'
jokes.setup: Ross cannot speak; his internal monologue escalates in panic
jokes.punchline: His internal exasperation reaches: 'This is the longest that anyone has not talked ever!' — a hyperbolic grammatically tortured sentence that itself reveals his mental state
jokes.explanation: Good escalation within the silence sequence. The sentence itself is slightly garbled — 'the longest that anyone has not talked ever' — which is perfect, because Ross is panicking. His academic precision breaking down under pressure is a character-specific detail.

jokes.text: Ross finally speaks: 'I haven't had sex in a very long time.'
jokes.setup: Ross's internal voice says 'There is nothing you could say to make this worse, so just say something!' — pressuring him to speak
jokes.punchline: He says 'I haven't had sex in a very long time.' — to his cousin, as a conversation opener
jokes.explanation: One of the funniest moments in the episode. The setup is extraordinary — Ross has been internally warned that NOTHING he says could make it worse. The punchline makes it instantly, maximally worse. 'I haven't had sex in a very long time' as an opener to your cousin — after an agonizing silence — is both completely in character for Ross (oversharing, socially disastrous) and an enormous laugh. The structure of 'nothing could make this worse' → immediately saying the worst thing possible is textbook, but executed at the highest level. Cassie's response ('Yeah, you really shouldn't have said anything') is the perfect button.

jokes.text: Cassie: 'Yeah, you really shouldn't have said anything.'
jokes.setup: Ross says 'I haven't had sex in a very long time' to his cousin
jokes.punchline: Cassie confirms what his internal voice just said was false: he definitely should not have said anything
jokes.explanation: Perfect button to joke #54. The echo of his internal monologue ('nothing you can say will make it worse' vs. 'you really shouldn't have said anything') is a beautiful structural callback. Deadpan, economical, devastating. Gets a high impact score as part of the sequence.

jokes.text: Monica's shower payoff: 'I get all those presents without talking to people I don't even like!'
jokes.setup: Monica generously says it works out for the best because she gets to spend the shower with the people she really loves
jokes.punchline: The sweet moment is immediately undercut by her real motivation: she gets presents without having to socialize with acquaintances she doesn't like
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom structure — the character builds to something sweet and then reveals the real, selfish motive. Monica's underlying pragmatism undercutting her emotional generosity is very in character. The punchline is a good laugh and the character work is solid.

jokes.text: Joey strips for the director, declaring 'I have nothing to hide. So, there you go. That's me. One hundred percent natural.' — then nothing happens for 25 seconds
jokes.setup: Joey believes he has successfully constructed a prosthetic and strips confidently for the director's inspection
jokes.punchline: An extended silent beat (20:05 to 20:30) where the director sees something wrong — the prosthetic has clearly failed — played entirely in silence and reaction
jokes.explanation: A masterful visual gag played entirely in silence and reaction. The audience knows the Silly Putty solution was fragile; Joey's confidence ('one hundred percent natural') followed by 25 seconds of nothing is devastating comedy. What the director sees — and what we don't see — is left to the imagination, which is funnier than showing it. 'That has never happened before' is the perfect button.

jokes.text: Joey: 'I tell you, that has never happened before.'
jokes.setup: The director has just witnessed something going wrong with Joey's prosthetic
jokes.punchline: Joey's embarrassed assurance that this has 'never happened before' — a phrase borrowed from sexual embarrassment that is perfectly inappropriate here
jokes.explanation: Excellent button to the visual gag. 'That has never happened before' is a phrase immediately recognizable from other embarrassing male situations, and its application to a Silly Putty prosthetic catastrophe is brilliantly wrong. Joey's sincerity in delivering it makes it land harder.

jokes.text: Ross's internal voice: 'What? Say something. Say anything. Ask her out! She's not your cousin!'
jokes.setup: Ross is again frozen, staring at Cassie
jokes.punchline: His internal voice escalates to 'Ask her out! She's not your cousin!' — his id explicitly contradicting his superego's earlier 'she's your cousin' warnings, with 'she IS your cousin' clearly being the fact
jokes.explanation: Great closing beat on the Ross subplot. His internal voice explicitly asserting 'she's not your cousin!' — which is factually incorrect — is the culmination of his entire story arc in the episode. The escalation from earlier 'she is your cousin' warnings to his id now overriding with false information is a perfect dark comedic conclusion. High character integration and a strong closer.

jokes.text: Ross finds himself alone with Cassie again and his inner voice fires up: 'What? Say something. Say anything. Ask her out! She's not your cousin!'
jokes.setup: Ross is at his apartment now with Cassie staying over. He's had the disastrous encounter already.
jokes.punchline: Ross's inner voice is at it again — this time the new argument is 'she's not YOUR cousin' (implying she's Monica's cousin, technically), grasping at any distinction.
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback capper — Ross hasn't learned anything. 'She's not your cousin!' as the new rationalization is a clever escalation: the previous rationalizations justified the attraction; this one tries to actually make it permissible. The logic is wrong (she is Monica's cousin, therefore a family cousin) but it's exactly the kind of reach Ross would make.

tmdb_overview: Joey auditions for a big movie role which will require him to appear naked. A problem arises, however, when the part calls for an uncircumcised man. Meanwhile, Rachel and Phoebe go through the trouble of organizing  a last minute bridal shower for Monica. And Ross becomes attracted to his cousin after she visits.
insight: Cringe-driven episode leans hard on character awkwardness over laugh density.
